chapter: Clubs, publishers, unions and life in Denver
title: Louis Armstrong's influence: trumpeters straining their voices and wearing handkerchiefs
summary: After Fletcher presented Louis in Harlem, trumpet players copied his gravel voice, hung handkerchiefs and talked like him.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Like -- now I'm going to tell you a funny story. You just brought it to my mind. You know, the first time Fletcher played the Apollo Theater in New York City. I don't know if it was Apollo or Roseland. But he had just brought up Louis Armstrong from King Oliver's (unintelligible) band. And Louis would be good, you know, sing with that big gravel voice, you know, and he would play the trumpet (unintelligible) and have a handkerchief hanging down, you know, as a selling this sort of thing. And after he played about a week in Harlem, where he was introduced by Fletcher to the public, You never saw so many trumpet players, as -- one of the guys in the band said this -- said, "Man, I never saw so many trumpet players (unintelligible) here in New York with their head they'd -- after hearing Louis, they'd sleep a day in -- out the window. They'd catch a cold to sound like Louis."

"What'd you say there, Pops?" One of those things, and For sure, I thought, you know. (Unintelligible), you know, in they'd be hoarse and get your gravel voice, you know, and I think the -- all of the stores that sold handkerchiefs did a great business --

-- because they went and bought up all the handkerchiefs so they could let them hang down like you'd walk down the street, Louis, you know. And, oh, man, he'd walk out, and guys that you'd known a long time, and you'd know how they talked, they'd say, "Hey, man, how you doing?" I'm okay there, pops. "Everything's fine, (UNintelligible) -- cool."

And you'd look at him because you knew you knew his face, you thought he was crazy, but you knew he was a trumpet player. He was trying to talk like Louis, sing like Louis, you know, this was the influence he had on the guys. But I thought it was funny when you said, "Man, you don't know how many trumpet players sleep with their head out the window in the rain to get hoarse to sound like Louis." That was a funny thing.
